An explicit stationary phase formula for the local formal Fourier-Laplace transform

Claude Sabbah Address: UMR 7640 du CNRS
Centre de Mathématiques Laurent Schwartz
École polytechnique
F–91128 Palaiseau cedex
France Email address: sabbah@math.polytechnique.fr URL: http://www.math.polytechnique.fr/˜sabbah
Abstract

We give an explicit formula (i.e., an explicit expression for the formal stationary phase formula) for the local Fourier-Laplace transform of a formal germ of meromorphic connection of one complex variable with a possibly irregular singularity.

Key words and phrases: 
Meromorphic connection, irregular singularity, local Fourier-Laplace transform, stationary phase formula
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 32S40; Secondary 14C30, 34Mxx

Introduction

We will denote by ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!) (resp. ℂ⁡({t})\mathbb{C}(\!\{t\}\!)) the field ℂ​[[t]]​[t−1]\mathbb{C}[\![t]\!][t^{-1}] (resp. ℂ​{t}​[t−1]\mathbb{C}\{t\}[t^{-1}]) of formal (resp. convergent) Laurent series of the variable tt, equipped with its usual derivation ∂t\partial_{t}.

Let MM be a finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space with a connection ∇\nabla. The local formal Laplace transform ℱ(0,∞)\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)} (also called Fourier transform in the literature) was introduced in [1, 4] by analogy with the ℓ\ell-adic local Fourier transform considered in [6]. One way to produce it is to choose a free ℂ⁡[t,t−1]\mathbb{C}[t,t^{-1}]-module ℳ\mathscr{M} of finite rank equipped with a connection ∇\nabla having poles at most at t=0t=0 and t=∞t=\infty, with a regular singularity at infinity, and such that (ℂ((t))⊗ℂ⁡[t,t−1]ℳ,1⊗∇)=(M,∇)(\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[t,t^{-1}]}\mathscr{M},1\otimes\nabla)=(M,\nabla). Considering ℳ\mathscr{M} as a ℂ[t]⟨∂t⟩\mathbb{C}[t]\langle\partial_{t}\rangle-module, its (global) Laplace transform F​ℳF\mathscr{M} is the same ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space equipped with the ℂ[τ]⟨∂τ⟩\mathbb{C}[\tau]\langle\partial_{\tau}\rangle-structure defined by the correspondence τ=∂t\tau=\partial_{t}, ∂τ=−t\partial_{\tau}=-t. Tensoring with ℂ⁡[τ,τ−1]\mathbb{C}[\tau,\tau^{-1}] gives a ℂ[τ,τ−1]⟨τ∂τ⟩\mathbb{C}[\tau,\tau^{-1}]\langle\tau\partial_{\tau}\rangle-module F​ℳ​[τ−1]F\mathscr{M}[\tau^{-1}], and renaming θ=τ−1\theta=\tau^{-1} (and setting θ∂θ=−τ∂τ\theta\partial_{\theta}=-\tau\partial_{\tau}), we regard F​ℳ​[τ−1]F\mathscr{M}[\tau^{-1}] as a ℂ[θ,θ−1]⟨θ∂θ⟩\mathbb{C}[\theta,\theta^{-1}]\langle\theta\partial_{\theta}\rangle-module. Lastly, we define ℱ(0,∞)​M\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}M as ℂ⁡((θ))⊗ℂ⁡[θ,θ−1]F​ℳ​[τ−1]\mathbb{C}(\!(\theta)\!)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[\theta,\theta^{-1}]}F\mathscr{M}[\tau^{-1}], equipped with its natural connection. This does not depend of the choices made.

The previous transform corresponds to using the kernel e−t/θe^{-t/\theta}, and is also denoted by ℱ−(0,∞)\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{-}. Its inverse transform is denoted by ℱ+(∞,0)\mathscr{F}^{(\infty,0)}_{+}. There are also pairs of inverse transforms (ℱ±(s,∞),ℱ∓(∞,s))(\mathscr{F}^{(s,\infty)}_{\pm},\mathscr{F}^{(\infty,s)}_{\mp}) for any s∈ℂs\in\mathbb{C} and (ℱ±(∞,∞),ℱ∓(∞,∞))(\mathscr{F}^{(\infty,\infty)}_{\pm},\mathscr{F}^{(\infty,\infty)}_{\mp}). If we denote by F±F_{\pm} the algebraic Laplace transform with kernel e±t​τe^{\pm t\tau} acting on a ℂ[t]⟨∂t⟩\mathbb{C}[t]\langle\partial_{t}\rangle-module ℳ\mathscr{M}, the local formal stationary phase formula of [1, 4] relies the formalization of the Laplace transform of ℳ\mathscr{M} at each of its singularities (00, s^∈ℂ∗\widehat{s}\in\mathbb{C}^{*}, ∞^\widehat{\infty}) with the local formal Laplace transforms of ℳ\mathscr{M} itself at its singularities 00, s∈ℂ∗s\in\mathbb{C}^{*}, ∞\infty. Decomposing with respect to slopes at infinity gives the following diagram:

Starting from a given ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space MM with connection, the explicit computation of ℱ(0,∞)​M\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}M (or of the other local transforms) by means of equations can be cumbersome (see however a simple example in §5.b). In this article, we show (Theorem 5.1) how to pass explicitly from the Turrittin-Levelt decomposition of MM to that of ℱ(0,∞)​M\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}M (and similarly for the other local transforms). We note that such formulas were already mentioned by G. Laumon [6, §2.6.3] and attributed to B. Malgrange, as a motivation for similar formulas in the ℓ\ell-adic situation. Such formulas do not seem to be explicitly written (nor proved) in the literature (see the remark below, however). In this article, we provide a geometric method for the proof.

After some preliminaries fixing notation (§1), we introduce elementary formal meromorphic connections and give their main properties (§2) and we recall in §3 the refined Turrittin-Levelt decomposition, as obtained in [1]. The results of §4 are mainly given in this article for a better understanding of the formulas in §5, but are not directly used in the proof of the main theorem (Theorem 5.1). Lastly, in §5.d, we give some consequences of the theorem of preservation of the index of rigidity, proved in [1] following the proof of [5] in the ℓ\ell-adic case.

Remark.

After this article was written up, Ricardo García López pointed out to me the preprint [3], where a similar calculation for local Fourier transforms is done in the ℓ\ell-adic case. The formulas we give in §5 are the complex analogues of that in [3]. Let us also mention the article [2], the results of which where obtained approximately at the same time as the results of the present article, and in an independent way. The methods developed in [2] are of a more computational flavour, while those in the present article emphasize the geometry of the formulas; we try in particular to explain in a more general context (cf. §4) the reason why the Legendre transform occurs in the formula for φ^\widehat{\varphi} of Theorem 5.1.

1. Preliminaries

1.a. Operations on vector spaces with connection

We work in the abelian category of ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector spaces with a connection usually denoted by ∇\nabla. This category has tensor products and duality in a natural way. We simply denote the action of ∇∂t\nabla_{\partial_{t}} as ∂t\partial_{t}. We usually omit, when there should be no confusion, the subscript denoting the field when using tensor products. It will be convenient to denote by 𝟏\mathbf{1} the field itself with its connection dd.

Let ρ∈u​ℂ​[[u]]\rho\in u\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!] with valuation p⩾1p\geqslant 1. We regard ρ\rho as a morphism of degree pp from the formal disc with coordinate uu to the formal disc with coordinate tt through the correspondence ρ:ℂ⁡[[t]]→ℂ⁡[[u]]\rho:\mathbb{C}[\![t]\!]\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!], t↦ρ⁡(u)t\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\rho(u).

Let MM be a finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space equipped with a connection ∇\nabla. The pull-back ρ+​M\rho^{+}M is the vector space ρ∗​M=ℂ⁡((u))⊗ℂ⁡((t))M\rho^{*}M=\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)}M equipped with the pull-back connection ρ∗∇\rho^{*}\nabla defined by ∂u(1⊗m)=ρ′​(u)⊗∂tm\partial_{u}(1\otimes m)=\rho^{\prime}(u)\otimes\partial_{t}m.

Let NN be a ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-vector space with connection. The push-forward ρ+​N\rho_{+}N is defined as follows:

(1.a)  the ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space ρ∗​N\rho_{*}N is the ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space NN equipped with the structure of ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space given by f⁡(t)⋅m:=f⁡(ρ⁡(u))​mf(t)\cdot m:=f(\rho(u))m,

(1.a)  the action of ∂t\partial_{t} is that of ρ′(u)−1∂u\rho^{\prime}(u)^{-1}\partial_{u}.

The projection formula holds:

ρ+​(N⊗ℂ⁡((u))ρ+​M)≃ρ+​N⊗ℂ⁡((t))M.\rho_{+}(N\otimes_{\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)}\rho^{+}M)\simeq\rho_{+}N\otimes_{\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)}M. (1.3)

If N∗N^{*} denotes Homℂ⁡((u))⁡(N,ℂ⁡((u)))\Hom_{\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)}(N,\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)) with its natural connection, we have ρ+​(N∗)≃(ρ+​N)∗\rho_{+}(N^{*})\simeq(\rho_{+}N)^{*}. Therefore we also have the projection formula

ρ+​Homℂ⁡((u))⁡(N,ρ+​M)≃Homℂ⁡((t))⁡(ρ+​N,M).\rho_{+}\Hom_{\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)}(N,\rho^{+}M)\simeq\Hom_{\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)}(\rho_{+}N,M).

Let φ∈ℂ⁡((u))\varphi\in\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!). We denote by ℰφ\mathscr{E}^{\varphi} the rank-one vector space ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!) equipped with the connection ∇=d+d​φ\nabla=d+d\varphi, i.e., such that ∇∂u1=φ′\nabla_{\partial_{u}}1=\varphi^{\prime}. We have ℰφ≃ℰψ\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\simeq\mathscr{E}^{\psi} if and only if φ≡ψmodℂ⁡[[u]]\varphi\equiv\psi\bmod\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!].

1.b. Moderate nearby cycles

Let XX a smooth complex algebraic variety and let f:X→𝔸1f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1} be a function on XX, defining a reduced divisor D=f−1​(0)D=f^{-1}(0). Let ℳ\mathscr{M} be a holonomic left 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module such that ℳ=𝒪X(∗D)⊗𝒪Xℳ\mathscr{M}=\mathscr{O}_{X}(*D)\otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}\mathscr{M} (we then say that ℳ\mathscr{M} is localized away from DD). The (moderate) nearby cycles module ψf​ℳ\psi_{f}\mathscr{M} is a holonomic left 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module supported on DD equipped with an automorphism T:ψf​ℳ→ψf​ℳT:\psi_{f}\mathscr{M}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\psi_{f}\mathscr{M}.

Let π:X′→X\pi:X^{\prime}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}X be a proper modification inducing an isomorphism X′∖π−1​(D)→X∖DX^{\prime}\smallsetminus\pi^{-1}(D)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}X\smallsetminus D and let us set f′=f∘πf^{\prime}=f\circ\pi, D′=π−1​(D)=f′−1​(0)D^{\prime}=\pi^{-1}(D)=f^{\prime-1}(0). If ℳ′\mathscr{M}^{\prime} is a holonomic left 𝒟X′\mathscr{D}_{X^{\prime}}-module localized away from D′D^{\prime}, we will denote by π+0​ℳ′\pi^{0}_{+}\mathscr{M}^{\prime} the holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module ℋ0π+ℳ′(∗D)\mathscr{H}^{0}\pi_{+}\mathscr{M}^{\prime}(*D). As a 𝒪X(∗D)\mathscr{O}_{X}(*D)-module, it is equal to π∗​ℳ′\pi_{*}\mathscr{M}^{\prime}.

As π\pi is proper, we have (see e.g., [12, 8])

ψfπ0+ℳ′≃ℋ0π|D′,+ψf′ℳ′,ℋjπ|D′,+ψf′ℳ′=0 if j≠0.\psi_{f}\pi^{0}_{+}\mathscr{M}^{\prime}\simeq\mathscr{H}^{0}\pi_{|D^{\prime},+}\psi_{f^{\prime}}\mathscr{M}^{\prime},\quad\mathscr{H}^{j}\pi_{|D^{\prime},+}\psi_{f^{\prime}}\mathscr{M}^{\prime}=0\text{ if }j\neq 0. (1.4)

Let us assume that XX is the affine space 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} with coordinates (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}) and that f⁡(x1,x2)=x1m1​x2m2=xmf(x_{1},x_{2})=x_{1}^{m_{1}}x_{2}^{m_{2}}=x^{m} with m1∈ℕm_{1}\in\mathbb{N} and m2∈ℕ∗m_{2}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Let us set D1={x2=0}D_{1}=\{x_{2}=0\} with coordinate x1x_{1} and D=|{xm=0}|D=|\{x^{m}=0\}|. Let ℛ\mathscr{R} be a locally free 𝒪X(∗D)\mathscr{O}_{X}(*D)-module of finite rank with a flat connection having regular singularitites along DD. Then ℛ\mathscr{R} is also a regular holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module. The 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module ψf​ℛ\psi_{f}\mathscr{R} is supported on DD. Moreover, if m1≠0m_{1}\neq 0, (ψf​ℛ)​[x1−1](\psi_{f}\mathscr{R})[x_{1}^{-1}] is supported on D1D_{1} and is the direct image (in the sense of left 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-modules) by the inclusion D1⸦→𝔸2D_{1}\mathrel{\lhook\joinrel\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}}\mathbb{A}^{2} of a regular holonomic 𝒟D1\mathscr{D}_{D_{1}}-module localized (and smooth) away from {x1=0}\{x_{1}=0\}. We will not distinguish between both, according to Kashiwara’s equivalence.

Proposition 1.5 (cf. [11, Lemma III.4.5.10]).

With the previous setting, for any λ∈ℂ∗\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^{*},

  1. (1)

    if n∈(ℕ∗)2n\in(\mathbb{N}^{*})^{2}, ψf​(ℰλ/xn⊗ℛ)=0\psi_{f}(\mathscr{E}^{\lambda/x^{n}}\otimes\mathscr{R})=0

  2. (2)

    if n1∈ℕ∗n_{1}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, ψf​(ℰλ/x1n1⊗ℛ)\psi_{f}(\mathscr{E}^{\lambda/x_{1}^{n_{1}}}\otimes\mathscr{R}) is supported on D1D_{1}; it is isomorphic to ℰλ/x1n1⊗((ψf​ℛ)​[x1−1])\mathscr{E}^{\lambda/x_{1}^{n_{1}}}\otimes\big((\psi_{f}\mathscr{R})[x_{1}^{-1}]\big) (with monodromy).∎

Let us note that 1.5(2) is stated in a weaker way in loc. cit, but the argument given in the proof gives 1.5(2).

2. Elementary formal meromorphic connections

Let MM be a finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space equipped with a connection ∇\nabla. The classical Turrittin-Levelt theorem asserts that, after a suitable ramification ρ:u↦t=up\rho:u\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}t=u^{p}, the pull-back ρ+​M\rho^{+}M can be decomposed into elementary formal connections ℰφ⊗Rφ\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R_{\varphi}, where φ∈ℂ⁡((u))\varphi\in\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!) and RφR_{\varphi} has a regular singularity. Moreover, it is known that MM itself can be decomposed according to the slopes of its Newton polygon (see, e.g., [7]).

In the next section, we refine the decomposition with respect to slopes, in order to keep as much information as possible from the Turrittin-Levelt decomposition, by using the elementary formal connections that we define now.

Definition 2.1 (Elementary formal connections).

Given ρ∈u​ℂ​[[u]]\rho\in u\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!], φ∈ℂ⁡((u))\varphi\in\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!) and a finite dimensional ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-vector space RR with regular connection ∇\nabla, we define the associated elementary finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space with connection by

El⁡(ρ,φ,R)=ρ+​(ℰφ⊗R).\El(\rho,\varphi,R)=\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R).

If pp denotes the order of ρ\rho, qq the order of the pole of φ\varphi and rr the rank of RR, then

  • ∙{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}

    El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) has only one slope, which is equal to q/pq/p,

  • ∙{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}

    the irregularity number irr0​El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\mathrm{irr}_{0}\El(\rho,\varphi,R) is equal to q​rqr,

  • ∙{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}

    the rank of El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) is equal to p​rpr.

Up to isomorphism, El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) only depends on φmodℂ⁡[[u]]\varphi\bmod\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!]. Standard results on regular formal meromorphic connections then show that, up to isomorphism, any elementary vector space El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) with connection is defined over the field of convergent series ℂ⁡({t})\mathbb{C}(\!\{t\}\!). Let us also note that giving RR is equivalent to giving a finite dimensional ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space equipped with an automorphism TT.

Let us first distinguish the isomorphism classes of the elementary finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector spaces with connection.

Lemma 2.2.

Assume that ρ′​(0)≠0\rho^{\prime}(0)\neq 0 (i.e., ρ\rho is an automorphism of the formal disc). Then El⁡(ρ,φ,R)≃El⁡(Id,ψ,S)\El(\rho,\varphi,R)\simeq\El(\Id,\psi,S) if and only if ψ∘ρ≡φmodℂ⁡[[u]]\psi\circ\rho\equiv\varphi\bmod\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!] and S≃RS\simeq R.

Proof.

Let us denote by λ\lambda the reciprocal series of ρ\rho, that is, ρ∘λ⁡(t)=t\rho\circ\lambda(t)=t, λ∘ρ⁡(u)=u\lambda\circ\rho(u)=u. We use that, ρ+=λ+\rho_{+}=\lambda^{+}. Then

El⁡(ρ,φ,R)=λ+​(ℰφ⊗R)=ℰφ∘λ⊗λ+​R≃ℰφ∘λ⊗R,\El(\rho,\varphi,R)=\lambda^{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R)=\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\lambda}\otimes\lambda^{+}R\simeq\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\lambda}\otimes R,

hence, tensoring with ℰ−ψ\mathscr{E}^{-\psi}, we find S≃ℰφ∘λ−ψ⊗RS\simeq\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\lambda-\psi}\otimes R, and the lemma follows easily. ∎

Let us come back to the general situation where ρ\rho has degree p⩾1p\geqslant 1. We deduce from the previous lemma that any elementary vector space El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) with connection is isomorphic to an elementary vector space El([u↦up],ψ,R)\El([u\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}u^{p}],\psi,R) with connection for a suitable ψ\psi. More precisely, if u↦λ⁡(u)u\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\lambda(u) is a formal automorphism (i.e., λ′​(0)≠0\lambda^{\prime}(0)\neq 0) then

El⁡(ρ,φ,R)≃El⁡(ρ∘λ,φ∘λ,R).\El(\rho,\varphi,R)\simeq\El(\rho\circ\lambda,\varphi\circ\lambda,R). (2.3)

Let us denote by ρ\rho the map u↦upu\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}u^{p} and by μζ\mu_{\zeta} the map u↦ζ​uu\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\zeta u.

Lemma 2.4.

For any φ∈ℂ⁡((u))\varphi\in\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!), we have

ρ+​ρ+​ℰφ=⨁ζp=1ℰφ∘μζ.\rho^{+}\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}=\mathop{\textstyle\bigoplus}\limits_{\zeta^{p}=1}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}}.
Proof.

We choose a ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-basis ee of ℰφ\mathscr{E}^{\varphi} and assume for simplicity that φ∈u−1​ℂ​[u−1]\varphi\in u^{-1}\mathbb{C}[u^{-1}]. Then the family e,u​e,…,up−1​ee,ue,\dots,u^{p-1}e is a ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-basis of ρ+​ℰφ\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}. Set ek=u−k⊗ℂ⁡((t))uk​ee_{k}=u^{-k}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)}u^{k}e. Then the family 𝒆=(e0,…,ep−1)\boldsymbol{e}=(e_{0},\dots,e_{p-1}) is a ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-basis of ρ+​ρ+​ℰφ\rho^{+}\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}. Let us decompose u​φ′​(u)=∑j=0p−1uj​ψj​(up)u\varphi^{\prime}(u)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}u^{j}\psi_{j}(u^{p}) with ψj∈ℂ⁡[t−1]\psi_{j}\in\mathbb{C}[t^{-1}] for any j⩾1j\geqslant 1 and ψ0∈t−1​ℂ​[t−1]\psi_{0}\in t^{-1}\mathbb{C}[t^{-1}]. Let P\mathrm{P} denote the permutation matrix defined by 𝒆⋅P=(e1,…,ep−1,e0)\boldsymbol{e}\cdot\mathrm{P}=(e_{1},\dots,e_{p-1},e_{0}). Using (1.a), we find that

u​∂uek=∑j=0p−k−1uj​ψj​ek+j+∑j=p−kp−1uj​ψj​ek+j−p,u\partial_{u}e_{k}=\sum_{j=0}^{p-k-1}u^{j}\psi_{j}e_{k+j}+\sum_{j=p-k}^{p-1}u^{j}\psi_{j}e_{k+j-p},

that is,

u​∂u𝒆=𝒆⋅[∑j=0p−1uj​ψj​Pj].u\partial_{u}\boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{e}\cdot\Big[\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}u^{j}\psi_{j}\mathrm{P}^{j}\Big].

The result is obtained by diagonalizing P\mathrm{P}. ∎

Remark 2.5.

Let us decompose pp as a product p=p′​dp=p^{\prime}d and ρ:u↦up\rho:u\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}u^{p} as ρd∘ρ′\rho_{d}\circ\rho^{\prime} correspondingly. Then ρd+​ρ+​ℰφ\rho_{d}^{+}\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi} decomposes as ⨁k=0,…,d−1ρ+′​ℰφ∘μexp⁡2​π​i​k/p\bigoplus_{k=0,\dots,d-1}\rho^{\prime}_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\mu_{\exp 2\pi ik/p}}. Indeed, this is obtained by writing ρ+​ρ+​ℰφ=ρ′⁣+​(ρd+​ρ+​ℰφ)\rho^{+}\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}=\rho^{\prime+}(\rho_{d}^{+}\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}) as the double direct sum of the terms ℰφ∘μexp⁡2​π​i​k/p∘μζ′\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\mu_{\exp 2\pi ik/p}\circ\mu_{\zeta^{\prime}}}, where ζ′\zeta^{\prime} varies among the p′p^{\prime}th roots of the unity and kk varies from 00 to d−1d-1.

Lemma 2.6.

We have El([u↦up],φ,R)≃El([u↦up],ψ,S)\El([u\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}u^{p}],\varphi,R)\simeq\El([u\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}u^{p}],\psi,S) if and only if the following properties are satisfied:

  1. (1)

    there exists ζ\zeta with ζp=1\zeta^{p}=1 and ψ∘μζ≡φmodℂ⁡[[u]]\psi\circ\mu_{\zeta}\equiv\varphi\bmod\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!],

  2. (2)

    S≃RS\simeq R as ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-vector spaces with connection.

Proof.

For the “if” part, notice that ρ=ρ∘μζ\rho=\rho\circ\mu_{\zeta}. We have μζ+​(ℰφ⊗R)≃ℰφ∘μζ⊗R\mu_{\zeta}^{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R)\simeq\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}}\otimes R, hence ℰφ⊗R≃μζ+​(ℰφ∘μζ⊗R)\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R\simeq\mu_{\zeta+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}}\otimes R), so ρ+​(ℰφ⊗R)≃ρ+​(ℰφ∘μζ⊗R)\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R)\simeq\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}}\otimes R).

For the “only if” part, let us choose a finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space with regular connection, that we denote by R1/pR^{1/p}, such that ρ+​R1/p=R\rho^{+}R^{1/p}=R (this amounts to choose a ppth root of an automorphism of a ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space). We then have

ρ+​(ℰφ⊗R)=ρ+​(ℰφ⊗ρ+​R1/p)=ρ+​ℰφ⊗R1/p,\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R)=\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes\rho^{+}R^{1/p})=\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R^{1/p},

hence ρ+​ρ+​(ℰφ⊗R)=(ρ+​ρ+​ℰφ)⊗R\rho^{+}\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R)=(\rho^{+}\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi})\otimes R. If ρ+​(ℰφ⊗R)≃ρ+​(ℰψ⊗S)\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R)\simeq\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\psi}\otimes S), we can lift this isomorphism after ρ+\rho^{+}. From Lemma 2.4 and the previous computation we deduce that ρ+​ρ+​(ℰφ⊗R)\rho^{+}\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R) decomposes as a sum of terms ℰφ∘μη⊗Rν\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\mu_{\eta}}\otimes R^{\nu}, where ν\nu is the number of ζ\zeta’s such that φ∘μζ≡φmodℂ⁡[[u]]\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}\equiv\varphi\bmod\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!], and where η\eta is such that ηp/ν=1\eta^{p/\nu}=1. It follows that (1) is satisfied and that Rν≃SνR^{\nu}\simeq S^{\nu}. Then R≃SR\simeq S (if two automorphisms T,T′T,T^{\prime} of a finite dimensional ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space are such that ⊕i=1νT\oplus_{i=1}^{\nu}T is conjugate to ⊕i=1νT′\oplus_{i=1}^{\nu}T^{\prime}, then TT and T′T^{\prime} are conjugate: this can be seen by considering the Jordan normal forms). ∎

Corollary 2.7.

Let El⁡(ρ1,φ1,R1)\El(\rho_{1},\varphi_{1},R_{1}) and El⁡(ρ2,φ2,R2)\El(\rho_{2},\varphi_{2},R_{2}) be two elementary formal connections with p1=p2=pp_{1}=p_{2}=p. Then El⁡(ρ1,φ1,R1)≃El⁡(ρ2,φ2,R2)\El(\rho_{1},\varphi_{1},R_{1})\simeq\El(\rho_{2},\varphi_{2},R_{2}) if and only if there exist ζ\zeta with ζp=1\zeta^{p}=1 and λ1,λ2∈u​ℂ​[[u]]\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\in u\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!] satisfying λ1′​(0)≠0\lambda^{\prime}_{1}(0)\neq 0 and λ2′​(0)≠0\lambda^{\prime}_{2}(0)\neq 0, such that

ρ1=ρ2∘λ1,φ1≡φ2∘λ1∘(λ2−1∘μζ∘λ2)modℂ⁡[[u]].\rho_{1}=\rho_{2}\circ\lambda_{1},\quad\varphi_{1}\equiv\varphi_{2}\circ\lambda_{1}\circ(\lambda_{2}^{-1}\circ\mu_{\zeta}\circ\lambda_{2})\mod\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!]. ∎
Remark 2.8.

Let El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) be an elementary formal connection and assume that there exists a decomposition ρ=ρ1∘ρ2\rho=\rho_{1}\circ\rho_{2} such that φ=φ1∘ρ2\varphi=\varphi_{1}\circ\rho_{2}. Then

ρ+​(ℰφ⊗R)=ρ1,+​ρ2,+​(ℰφ1∘ρ2⊗R)=ρ1,+​(ℰφ1⊗R1)\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R)=\rho_{1,+}\rho_{2,+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi_{1}\circ\rho_{2}}\otimes R)=\rho_{1,+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi_{1}}\otimes R_{1})

where R1=ρ2,+​RR_{1}=\rho_{2,+}R has a regular singularity. In other word, El⁡(ρ,φ,R)=El⁡(ρ1,φ1,R1)\El(\rho,\varphi,R)=\El(\rho_{1},\varphi_{1},R_{1}). Hence it is always possible to choose the presentation of an elementary formal connection in a minimal way, such that φ\varphi cannot be defined on a ramified sub-covering of ρ\rho. We will the say that ρ\rho is minimal with respect to φ\varphi.

Determinant

We now give a formula for the determinant of El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R). Recall that, if MM is any finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-module with connection, the determinant detM\det M is equipped with a natural connection and, if AA is the matrix of ∇∂t\nabla_{\partial_{t}} in some basis of MM, then the matrix of ∇∂t\nabla_{\partial_{t}} acting on detM\det M is Tr⁡A\Tr A. If the connection on MM is regular, then the connection on detM\det M is completely determined by the residue of its connection modulo ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Proposition 2.9.

The determinant of of the elementary ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-module with connection El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) is isomorphic to ℰr​Tr⁡φ⊗detR⊗(t(p−1)​r/2)\mathscr{E}^{r\Tr\varphi}\otimes\det R\otimes(t^{(p-1)r/2}), where pp is the degree of ρ\rho, rr is the rank of RR, (t(p−1)​r/2)(t^{(p-1)r/2}) is the rank one free ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-module with connection d+[(p−1)​r/2]​d​t/td+[(p-1)r/2]dt/t, and detR\det R is the rank one ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-module detR\det R where we change the name of the variable uu to tt.

Proof.

As RR is a successive extension of rank-one free ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-modules with regular connection, we can reduce to the case RR has rank one. We can also assume that ρ⁡(u)=up\rho(u)=u^{p}. If φ∈ℂ⁡((u))\varphi\in\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!), we denote by φinv\varphi^{\mathrm{inv}} its invariant part with respect to the action of ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}.

If ee is a ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-basis of the rank-one module ℰφ⊗R\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R, then e,u​e,…,up−1​ee,ue,\dots,u^{p-1}e is a ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-basis of ρ∗​(ℰφ⊗R)\rho_{*}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R). If α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C} is the residue of (R,∇)(R,\nabla), then the matrix of the action of t∂tt\partial_{t} in this basis is given by

1p[αId+diag(0,…,p−1)+uφu′⋅]\frac{1}{p}\big[\alpha\Id+\diag(0,\dots,p-1)+u\varphi^{\prime}_{u}\cdot{}\big]

where the multiplication by u​φu′u\varphi^{\prime}_{u} has to be interpreted as an operator on the ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-module ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!). We note that multiplication by uℓu^{\ell} on ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!) has trace zero except when ℓ\ell is a multiple of pp. Thus 1pTr[uφu′⋅]=1pTr([uφu′⋅]inv)=t(Trφ)t′\frac{1}{p}\Tr[u\varphi^{\prime}_{u}\cdot{}]=\frac{1}{p}\Tr([u\varphi^{\prime}_{u}\cdot{}]^{\mathrm{inv}})=t(\Tr\varphi)^{\prime}_{t}. Therefore, the trace of the matrix of the action of t∂tt\partial_{t} on the basis e,…,up−1​ee,\dots,u^{p-1}e is

α+p−12+t​(Tr⁡φ)t′.∎\alpha+\frac{p-1}{2}+t(\Tr\varphi)^{\prime}_{t}.\qed
Corollary 2.10.

If slope​El⁡(ρ,φ,R)<1\textup{slope}\El(\rho,\varphi,R)<1, then detEl⁡(ρ,φ,R)\det\El(\rho,\varphi,R) has a regular singularity.

Proof.

Indeed, q<pq<p implies Tr⁡φ=0modℂ⁡[[t]]\Tr\varphi=0\bmod\mathbb{C}[\![t]\!]. ∎

3. Formal decomposition of a germ of meromorphic connection

Proposition 3.1.

Any irreducible finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space MM with connection is isomorphic to ρ+​(ℰφ⊗L)\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes L), where φ∈u−1​ℂ​[u−1]\varphi\in u^{-1}\mathbb{C}[u^{-1}], ρ:u↦t=up\rho:u\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}t=u^{p} has degree p⩾1p\geqslant 1 and is minimal with respect to φ\varphi (cf. Remark 2.8), and LL is some rank one ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-vector space with regular connection.

Proof.

Assume that MM is irreducible. According to the classical Turrittin-Levelt theorem, we can choose ρ:u↦t=up\rho:u\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}t=u^{p} such that ρ+​M\rho^{+}M decomposes as ⊕φ(ℰφ⊗Rφ)\oplus_{\varphi}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R_{\varphi}). We have a natural action of ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} on ρ+​M\rho^{+}M, and MM is recovered as the invariant subspace. Therefore, by irreducibility, there exists φ∈ℂ⁡((u))\varphi\in\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!) such that ρ+M≃⊕ζp=1(ℰφ∘μζ⊗Rφ∘μζ)\rho^{+}M\simeq\oplus_{\zeta^{p}=1}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}}\otimes R_{\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}}) and we can assume that pp is minimal, so that for any ζ≠1\zeta\neq 1 with ζp=1\zeta^{p}=1, we have φ∘μζ≢φmodℂ⁡[[u]]\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}\not\equiv\varphi\bmod\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!]. The ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}-action induces isomorphisms aζ:Rφ→Rφ∘μζa_{\zeta}:R_{\varphi}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}R_{\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}} which compose themselves in the right way. Let us set R=RφR=R_{\varphi} and let us choose R1/pR^{1/p} as in the proof of Lemma 2.6. Then ρ+​M≃ρ+​(ρ+​ℰφ⊗R1/p)\rho^{+}M\simeq\rho^{+}(\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R^{1/p}) and, taking the ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}-invariant part, we get M≃ρ+​ℰφ⊗R1/pM\simeq\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R^{1/p}. Still by irreducibility, R1/pR^{1/p}, hence RR, has rank one.

On the other hand, such a ρ+​(ℰφ⊗L)\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes L) is irreducible: indeed, ρ+​ρ+​(ℰφ⊗L)\rho^{+}\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes L) decomposes as the direct sum of rank-one non-isomorphic connections, and has no non-trivial ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}-invariant submodule. ∎

Remark 3.2.

There is no unique way, in general, to write down an irreducible meromorphic connection: either we choose the presentation ρ+​(ℰφ⊗ℂ⁡((u))L)\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)}L), and LL is uniquely defined up to isomorphism, but φ\varphi could be changed into φ∘μζ\varphi\circ\mu_{\zeta}, or we choose ρ+​(ℰφ)⊗ℂ⁡((t))L1/p\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi})\otimes_{\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)}L^{1/p}, and L1/pL^{1/p} is not uniquely defined. We will call ρ+​ℰφ\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi} the exponential irreducibility type of the irreducible meromorphic connection.

Corollary 3.3 (Refined Turrittin-Levelt, cf. [1]).

Any finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space MM with connection can be written in a unique way as a direct sum ⨁El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\bigoplus\El(\rho,\varphi,R), in such a way that each ρ+​ℰφ\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi} is irreducible and no two ρ+​ℰφ\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi} are isomorphic.

Proof.

Fix an irreducible ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-module II with connection and consider in MM the II-typical component MIM_{I} defined as the maximal submodule such that all irreducible sub-quotients are isomorphic to I⊗LI\otimes L for some rank one regular ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-module with connection LL. It will be convenient to choose II as ρ+​ℰφ\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi} for some suitable ρ\rho and φ\varphi as in Proposition 3.1. Then, if I1≄I2I_{1}\not\simeq I_{2}, there is no non-zero morphism from MI1M_{I_{1}} to MI2M_{I_{2}}, and we get the decomposition M=⊕IMIM=\oplus_{I}M_{I}. On the other hand, each MIM_{I} is isomorphic to ρ+​(ℰφ⊗R)\rho_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{\varphi}\otimes R) for some regular RR. ∎

Corollary 3.4.

Let MM be a finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space with connection. Then MM is isomorphic to an elementary module El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) if and only if ρ+​M\rho^{+}M is isomorphic to ρ+​El⁡(ρ,φ,R)=(ρ+​ρ+​ℰφ)⊗R\rho^{+}\El(\rho,\varphi,R)=(\rho^{+}\rho_{+}\mathscr{E}^{\varphi})\otimes R.∎

Corollary 3.5.

Let El⁡(ρ1,φ1,R1)\El(\rho_{1},\varphi_{1},R_{1}) and El⁡(ρ2,φ2,R2)\El(\rho_{2},\varphi_{2},R_{2}) be two elementary connections written in a minimal way (cf. Remark 2.8). Then El⁡(ρ1,φ1,R1)≃El⁡(ρ2,φ2,R2)\El(\rho_{1},\varphi_{1},R_{1})\simeq\El(\rho_{2},\varphi_{2},R_{2}) if and only if p1=p2p_{1}=p_{2} and the condition of Corollary 2.7 applies.

Proof.

Any irreducible sub-quotient of El⁡(ρ1,φ1,R1)\El(\rho_{1},\varphi_{1},R_{1}) takes the form El⁡(ρ1,φ1,L1)\El(\rho_{1},\varphi_{1},L_{1}) where L1L_{1} is a rank one sub-quotient of R1R_{1}. A similar result holds for El⁡(ρ2,φ2,R2)\El(\rho_{2},\varphi_{2},R_{2}). Each such sub-quotient has rank p1p_{1} (resp. p2p_{2}). It follows that p1=p2p_{1}=p_{2}. We can then apply Corollary 2.7. ∎

Remark 3.6 (Extension to 𝒟^\widehat{\mathscr{D}}-modules).

Let us denote by 𝒟^\widehat{\mathscr{D}} the ring of differential operators with coefficients in ℂ⁡[[t]]\mathbb{C}[\![t]\!]. Then any given holonomic 𝒟^\widehat{\mathscr{D}}-module MM can be decomposed as Mreg⊕MirrM_{\mathrm{reg}}\oplus M_{\mathrm{irr}}, where MregM_{\mathrm{reg}} is a regular holonomic 𝒟^\widehat{\mathscr{D}}-module and MirrM_{\mathrm{irr}} is purely irregular. Then MirrM_{\mathrm{irr}} is a ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-module with connection (although MregM_{\mathrm{reg}} may be not), and has the refined Turrittin-Levelt decomposition of Corollary 3.3, where all φ\varphi are non-zero in ℂ⁡((u))/ℂ⁡[[u]]\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)/\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!].

Let RR be a regular ℂ⁡((u))\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!)-module corresponding to a vector space with monodromy (ψu​R,T)(\psi_{u}R,T). 4. Direct images of exponentially twisted regular 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules

In this section we explain an improvement, in a particular case, of the main result of [10]. Let Δ\Delta be a disc centered at the origin in ℂ\mathbb{C} with coordinate tt and let ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} be the projective line with affine chart 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1} having coordinate xx. We denote by ∞\infty the point with coordinate x=∞x=\infty. Let ℳ\mathscr{M} be a regular holonomic 𝒟Δ×ℙ1\mathscr{D}_{\Delta\times\mathbb{P}^{1}}-module. In the following, we always assume that ℳ\mathscr{M} is equal to its localized module along the divisor [Δ×{∞}]∪[{0}×ℙ1][\Delta\times\{\infty\}]\cup[\{0\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}] (the adjunction of this second component will not affect the computation of the irregularity we are interested to compute). Let t:Δ×ℙ1→Δt:\Delta\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\Delta be the projection and let ℰx\mathscr{E}^{x} denotes the free rank-one 𝒪Δ×ℙ1(∗∞)\mathscr{O}_{\Delta\times\mathbb{P}^{1}}(*\infty)-module with connection d+d​xd+dx. The main result of [10] gives much information on the formal irregular part ℋ0​t+​(ℰx⊗ℳ)irr\mathscr{H}^{0}t_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{x}\otimes\mathscr{M})^{\mathrm{irr}} of ℋ0​t+​(ℰx⊗ℳ)\mathscr{H}^{0}t_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{x}\otimes\mathscr{M}) at the origin of Δ\Delta. Let us recall the notation of loc. cit.

The singular support of ℳ\mathscr{M} away from {0}×ℙ1\{0\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} (i.e., the locus where ℳ\mathscr{M} is not locally a vector bundle with flat connection away from {0}×ℙ1\{0\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}) is a germ along {0}×ℙ1\{0\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} of a analytic closed analytic set of Δ×ℙ1\Delta\times\mathbb{P}^{1} of dimension ⩽1\leqslant 1. Therefore, if Δ\Delta is small enough, it is a union of germs, at a finite number of points of {0}×ℙ1\{0\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}, of possibly singular complex analytic curves (distinct from {0}×ℙ1\{0\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}). We will denote by SS the germ at (0,∞)∈Δ×ℙ1(0,\infty)\in\Delta\times\mathbb{P}^{1} of the singular support of ℳ\mathscr{M} away from {0}×ℙ1\{0\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}. Let us denote by y=1/xy=1/x the coordinate at ∞\infty on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. We first make the following assumption:

Assumption 4.1.

The germ of SS at (0,∞)(0,\infty) is irreducible.

We fix a Puiseux parametrization of SS as t=upt=u^{p}, μ⁡(u)​y=uq\mu(u)y=u^{q} where μ\mu is holomorphic and μ⁡(0)≠0\mu(0)\neq 0. We assume that pp is minimal, in the sense that one cannot find a Puiseux parametrization of SS with a smaller pp. The inverse image ρ−1​S\rho^{-1}S of SS by ρ:(u,y)↦(up,y)\rho:(u,y)\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}(u^{p},y) consists of pp distinct smooth curves SζS_{\zeta} having equation ζ−q​μ​(ζ​u)​y=uq\zeta^{-q}\mu(\zeta u)y=u^{q}, where ζ\zeta varies among the ppth roots of the unity. In particular, the restriction of ρ\rho to any of the curves SζS_{\zeta} is isomorphic to the normalization ν:S~→S\nu:\widetilde{S}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}S.

We define α\alpha to be the polar part of u−q​μ​(u)u^{-q}\mu(u), and δ\delta to be its holomorphic part. If ζ\zeta varies among the ppth roots of the unity, the functions ζ−q​μ​(ζ​u)\zeta^{-q}\mu(\zeta u) are thus pairwise distinct. We will make the more restrictive following assumption, which is satisfied if (p,q)=1(p,q)=1:

Assumption 4.2.

The polar parts α⁡(ζ​u)\alpha(\zeta u) are pairwise distinct when ζ\zeta varies in the set of ppth roots of the unity.

Let us consider the de Rham complex DR⁡ℳ\DR\mathscr{M}. Fixing a local equation hh of SS at (0,∞)(0,\infty), we can define a constructible complex on SS by taking the vanishing cycle complex ϕh​DR⁡ℳ\phi_{h}\DR\mathscr{M}, whose natural monodromy around h=0h=0 we forget. Up to a shift (depending on the convention we took for perverse sheaves and vanishing cycle functor), the restriction of this complex to S∗:=S∖{(0,∞)}S^{*}:=S\smallsetminus\{(0,\infty)\} is a local system. Let ν:S~→S\nu:\widetilde{S}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}S be the normalization. The previous local system defines thus a vector bundle RR with meromorphic connection having a regular singularity at the origin of S~\widetilde{S}.

Theorem 4.3.

If SS is irreducible at (0,∞)(0,\infty) and if Assumption 4.2 is satisfied, the formal irregular part ℋ0​t+​(ℰx⊗ℳ)irr\mathscr{H}^{0}t_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{x}\otimes\mathscr{M})^{\mathrm{irr}} at the origin of Δ\Delta is isomorphic to El⁡(t∘ν,x∘ν,R)\El(t\circ\nu,x\circ\nu,R).

We assume that SS is non-empty, otherwise we know from [10] that ℋ0​t+​(ℰx⊗ℳ)\mathscr{H}^{0}t_{+}(\mathscr{E}^{x}\otimes\mathscr{M}) has a regular singularity at t=0t=0. 5. Local Laplace transform

5.a. The local Laplace transform ℱ(0,∞)\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}

In this section, we analyze the formal Laplace transform ℱ±(0,∞)\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{\pm} introduced in [1, 4]. Let us recall that, given a finite dimensional ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space MM with connection, its transform ℱ±(0,∞)​M\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{\pm}M is a finite dimensional ℂ⁡((θ))\mathbb{C}(\!(\theta)\!)-vector space with connection, where θ\theta is a new variable. The functor ℱ±(0,∞)\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{\pm} morally corresponds to the integral transform ∫∙e±t/θdt\int{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}\,e^{\pm t/\theta}dt. If ι\iota denotes the germ of formal automorphism t↦−tt\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}-t, we have ℱ+(0,∞)​M=ℱ−(0,∞)​ι+​M\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{+}M=\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{-}\iota^{+}M. Let us note that, if RR is regular, then ι+​R≃R\iota^{+}R\simeq R.

Theorem 5.1.

For any elementary ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)-vector space El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\El(\rho,\varphi,R) with irregular connection (i.e., such that φ∉ℂ⁡[[u]]\varphi\not\in\mathbb{C}[\![u]\!]), the formal Laplace transform ℱ±(0,∞)​El⁡(ρ,φ,R)\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{\pm}\El(\rho,\varphi,R) is the elementary finite dimensional ℂ⁡((θ))\mathbb{C}(\!(\theta)\!)-vector space with connection El⁡(ρ^±,φ^,R^)\El(\widehat{\rho}_{\pm},\widehat{\varphi},\widehat{R}) with (setting Lq=(ℂ⁡((u)),d−q2​d​uu)L_{q}=(\mathbb{C}(\!(u)\!),d-\tfrac{q}{2}\,\tfrac{du}{u}))

ρ^±​(u)=∓ρ′​(u)φ′​(u),φ^​(u)=φ⁡(u)−ρ⁡(u)ρ′​(u)​φ′​(u),R^≃R⊗Lq.\widehat{\rho}_{\pm}(u)=\mp\frac{\rho^{\prime}(u)}{\varphi^{\prime}(u)},\quad\widehat{\varphi}(u)=\varphi(u)-\frac{\rho(u)}{\rho^{\prime}(u)}\,\varphi^{\prime}(u),\quad\widehat{R}\simeq R\otimes L_{q}.
Remark 5.2 (Regular connections).

If RR is a regular connection, then it is easy to check that ℱ±(0,∞)​R≃R\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{\pm}R\simeq R (after replacing the name of the variable tt with θ\theta). This also explains why R^\widehat{R} does not depend on ±\pm in the formula above.

We will prove the theorem for the transform ℱ−(0,∞)\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{-}. The other case is obtained by setting ℱ+(0,∞)=ℱ−(0,∞)∘ι+\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{+}=\mathscr{F}^{(0,\infty)}_{-}\circ\iota^{+}. In the following, when we forget the index ±\pm, we implicitly work in the −- case.

A possible way of proving the theorem, by applying Theorem 4.3 to MM, would be to compute the vanishing cycle module of MM along SS. Let us compute directly the local Laplace transform of ℰa/tq\mathscr{E}^{a/t^{q}} for a∈ℂ∗a\in\mathbb{C}^{*} and q∈ℕ∗q\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Using that θ2∂θθ−1=θ∂θ−1\theta^{2}\partial_{\theta}\theta^{-1}=\theta\partial_{\theta}-1, it has the equation (θ2∂θ)q(θ∂θ−1)+qa(\theta^{2}\partial_{\theta})^{q}(\theta\partial_{\theta}-1)+qa. (ηq+1η∂η)q(η∂η−(q+1))+(−1)q[q(q+1)a]q+1=∏k=1q+1(ηq+1∂η−kηq)+(−1)q[q(q+1)a]q+1.(\eta^{q+1}\eta\partial_{\eta})^{q}(\eta\partial_{\eta}-(q+1))+(-1)^{q}[q(q+1)a]^{q+1}\\[-5.0pt] =\prod_{k=1}^{q+1}(\eta^{q+1}\partial_{\eta}-k\eta^{q})+(-1)^{q}[q(q+1)a]^{q+1}.

∏k=1q+1(ηq+1∂η−qλ−kηq)+(−1)q[q(q+1)a]q+1.\prod_{k=1}^{q+1}(\eta^{q+1}\partial_{\eta}-q\lambda-k\eta^{q})+(-1)^{q}[q(q+1)a]^{q+1}.

[−q(q+1)a]q(q+1)[η∂η−q+22].[-q(q+1)a]^{q}(q+1)\Big[\eta\partial_{\eta}-\frac{q+2}{2}\Big].
